upstream.note: The revision every upstream citation below was read at, and the ref docs/PARITY_GAP_ANALYSIS.md pins. Cite it with the commit, not the tag: `git show <commit>:cmd/tailscale/cli/ip.go` reproduces the rows, and a reader who resolves a bare path against main instead will find something else there and read the audit as stale.

summary.note: This edition replaces the previous one, which audited the ten CLI parity ports merged after PRs #293-#304. These ten rows are the ports merged after that edition (#459 through #482), each re-read diff-by-diff against a shallow clone of github.com/tailscale/tailscale at v1.102.4. Two are faithful, eight carry at least one divergence from the upstream behaviour their own diff claims to port, and eleven findings are recorded with the Go path and ref each was read at. The previous edition's rows and findings remain in git history.

auditedPrs.notes: The three-source auth-key precedence and all four of Go's gates (state != Running, conf == nil, no profiles or NeedsLogin) are ported faithfully, and the fork's whitespace ruling changes no outcome because Go's trimmed value is empty on that path too. The one behavioural divergence is on the reporting surface: the key's Value column carries the literal <redacted>, where Go's syspolicy list prints the decoded value for every key without exception.

Test-and-data only: it rewrites PARITY_AUDIT.json and the contract test over it, and claims no port of any Go behaviour. Nothing in the diff touches production code, so there is no upstream behaviour for it to diverge from. The audit content it carried is superseded by this edition rather than re-verified line by line.

The peer and Service arms now match runIP exactly: the empty-list check runs before the family check, and the returned text reaches stderr bare. Three refusals in the same ported function still answer differently. The self arm short-circuits on the daemon's own error reply, so a stopped node reads `error: node is not up` instead of Go's empty-list sentence; --assert prints fork wording; and the mutual-exclusion refusal still goes out through main's Result, so it carries the `Error: ` prefix Go never prints.

The central claim holds: an explicit [] now withdraws the routes, an absent or null key leaves them alone, the wrapper is applied once, and the non-masked refusal formats the parsed prefix. The neighbouring arm of the same ToPrefs block is not ported: AdvertiseExitNode with no AdvertiseRoutes key replaces the routes upstream and merely sets a separate bool here. And the refusal set run on the config path is wider than ToPrefs's, because it still includes the net/netutil route rules Go applies only in the CLI.

The ported step is right: status then prefs, the log line and its address rendering, the wrapped failure, setRunWebClient(true) before the mode split, and the interrupt arm gated on listener mode plus a pref this run turned on. What the diff does not carry over is the other half of the flag it introduced: upstream's --readonly also selects ReadOnlyServerMode and its absence selects LoginServerMode, while here the flag only decides whether the daemon pref is touched.

The framing is now Go's (cause, blank line, help pointer, exit 1), cleanURLPath runs at Go's position with Go's wrapper, the --service build gap moved behind Go's own checks, and the !forService half of the --tun condition is live. But the sequence the diff documents itself as reproducing names verifyFunnelEnabled, and no port of it exists anywhere in the tree, so funnel accepts ports and nodes upstream refuses before it ever looks at the listener flags.

go_io_error_text and go_mkdir_all are accurate ports, and the three reported call sites — the writability probe, the MkdirAll arm and the bare non-NotExist stat arm — are fixed. Two sibling call sites in the very function the diff rewrites were left on Rust's io::Error Display, so `reading kubeconfig` and the final open-for-write still print ` (os error N)` and still use fork wording rather than Go's.

The verification is sound on the half it checks: the nil-versus-empty rule, the skip-an-undecodable-list error path and the withholding itself all match fillAllowedSuggestions and refreshAllowedSuggestions. The commit is also candid that the ranking half is unbuildable here and files it as an engine ask. That unbuilt half is a behavioural divergence all the same, because suggestExitNodeUsingDERP filters candidates before it ranks them and still returns a permitted node where this build returns nothing.

Docs, one module-doc note, one guard-test entry and one test over a profile-less state dir. No behaviour changes. The precedence it documents is the order upstream's Start actually uses — the policy key is read only after an explicit key and after the config file's own AuthKey — so the design doc now agrees with both the code and upstream.

The completion and the colon rule are reproduced exactly, clause for clause, including the decision to test for a colon rather than a tag: prefix, and both daemon entry points apply it before anything is persisted. The commit's claim that the message shape is aligned to upstream's `tag: %q` does not hold: every refusal here is reworded, so both the wrapper and all four CheckTag clauses read differently from Go.

gate.detail: Run on main at b41721d. `cargo fmt --all --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean; `cargo build --release --bins` finished. `cargo test --all-targets` failed once on this machine only: tests::cleanup_refuses_live_socket panicked with `path must be shorter than SUN_LEN` because the test binds a Unix socket under std::env::temp_dir(), which is 66 characters here and overruns the 104-byte macOS sun_path limit. Re-run with a short TMPDIR the whole suite is green: 1158 passed, 0 failed, 0 targets skipped. The failure is the environment, not the tree.

findings.title: The addressless case the PR is named for is still unreachable on a stopped node
findings.detail: Upstream runIP reads Status once and, whatever the node's state, reaches `if len(ips) == 0 { return fmt.Errorf("no current Tailscale IPs; state: %v", st.BackendState) }` — so `tailscale ip` on a stopped node prints `no current Tailscale IPs; state: Stopped` and exits 1. The merged self arm asks the daemon for `Request::Ip` first and, on `Response::Error`, prints `error: <daemon message>` and exits before any of the ported logic runs. A stopped node answers that request with an error, so it reads `error: node is not up` — the daemon's wording, with an `error: ` prefix Go does not use, and without the BackendState Go names. The empty-list sentence the diff added is only reachable when the daemon answers successfully with no addresses.

findings.title: verifyFunnelEnabled is in the documented order but not in the tree
findings.detail: runServeCombined calls `e.verifyFunnelEnabled(ctx, 443)` for the funnel subcommand between its two --service refusals and before cleanURLPath and srvTypeAndPortFromFlags. That call runs enableFeatureInteractive and then ipn.CheckFunnelAccess / ipn.CheckFunnelPort against the self node, so upstream refuses a funnel on a node without the https and funnel attributes, and refuses a port outside the Funnel-allowed set, before it ever looks at the listener flags. check_serve_flags documents itself as running serve_v2.go's checks in serve_v2.go's order and the merge message lists verifyFunnelEnabled in that sequence, but no port of it, of CheckFunnelAccess or of CheckFunnelPort exists in the crate. `tnet funnel --https=9000 3000` is therefore configured and reported as enabled where `tailscale funnel` refuses it; the two --service refusals also sit adjacent here rather than straddling the funnel check.

findings.title: AdvertiseExitNode with no AdvertiseRoutes key does not replace the routes
findings.detail: ToPrefs handles the two fields as one masked pref. When AdvertiseExitNode is true and AdvertiseRoutes was absent, `mp.AdvertiseRoutes = tsaddr.ExitRoutes(); mp.AdvertiseRoutesSet = true` — so the node ends up advertising exactly the two default routes and any previously persisted subnet routes are dropped. The merged apply_to_prefs models the exit node as its own boolean and only assigns advertise_routes inside `if let Some(routes) = &c.advertise_routes`, so the same config leaves the persisted subnet routes in place beside the exit-node intent. A node advertising 192.0.2.0/24 that is handed a config of {"AdvertiseExitNode": true} keeps advertising 192.0.2.0/24 here and stops advertising it upstream.

findings.title: Two call sites in the rewritten function still print Rust's io::Error text
findings.detail: setKubeconfigForPeer returns `fmt.Errorf("reading kubeconfig: %w", err)` for a non-NotExist read failure — no path in the wrapper, because the *os.PathError already carries one — and returns the os.WriteFile failure completely bare, as `open <path>: permission denied`. The merged set_kubeconfig_for_peer routes neither through go_io_error_text: the read arm uses `.with_context(|| format!("reading kubeconfig {path}"))` and the write arm `.with_context(|| format!("opening kubeconfig {path} for writing"))`, both over the raw io::Error. A kubeconfig whose parent is readable but whose file is mode 0400 therefore still prints `opening kubeconfig /home/x/.kube/config for writing: Permission denied (os error 13)` — the exact ` (os error N)` suffix and capitalised reason this change exists to remove, on the one line an operator hits most.

findings.title: Upstream filters candidates before ranking; this build withholds the ranked answer
findings.detail: suggestExitNodeUsingDERP applies the allow list inside its candidate loop — `if allowList != nil && !allowList.Contains(peer.StableID()) { continue }` — so the ranking runs over the permitted nodes only and returns the best permitted exit node. The merged path lets the engine rank over every candidate and then has diag::permitted_suggestion withhold the answer when the winner is excluded. On a tailnet with an excluded node and a permitted one, upstream suggests the permitted node and this build suggests nothing. The empty result upstream returns is the case where no candidate passes the filter at all, which is not the same case. The commit says so and files the ranking half as an engine ask; the divergence is recorded here because it is still a difference in what an administrator's managed node answers.

findings.title: syspolicy list renders the AuthKey as <redacted> where Go prints its value
findings.detail: runSysPolicyList formats every configured setting with `fmt.Fprintf(w, "%s\t%s\t%v\t\n", k, origin, setting.Value())` and has no special case for pkey.AuthKey, so upstream prints the administrator's key in the Value column like any other string setting. The merged read_source substitutes the literal <redacted> for that one key and carries the usable copy out of band. The row still reports that the key is configured and which store supplied it, and the reasoning is sound, but the ported report no longer reproduces the output of the command it ports, and an administrator cannot confirm from tnet which key arrived.

findings.title: The config path enforces net/netutil route rules ToPrefs does not have
findings.detail: ToPrefs's AdvertiseRoutes block refuses exactly one thing — a prefix with non-address bits set — and nothing else, so a Go config of {"AdvertiseRoutes": ["0.0.0.0/0"]} is accepted and applied. The counterpart rule and the 4-in-6 minimum-length rule live in net/netutil/routes.go, which the CLI's up and set call and ipn/conf.go never does. The merged apply_to_prefs runs validate_advertise_routes, which carries all three, and the same diff puts Go's ToPrefs wrapper `error parsing config to prefs: ` in front of them — so this build refuses a config upstream accepts, and attributes the refusal to a function that never produced it.

findings.title: The tag refusals are reworded, so `tag: %q` alignment is not what shipped
findings.detail: prefsFromUpArgs wraps every CheckTag failure as `fmt.Errorf("tag: %q: %s", tag, err)`, and tailcfg.CheckTag supplies four exact sentences: `tags must start with 'tag:'`, `tag names must not be empty`, `tag names must start with a letter, after 'tag:'` and `tag names can only contain numbers, letters, or dashes`. complete_and_validate_advertise_tags reproduces the completion and the colon rule faithfully but rewrites all five strings — the wrapper reads `invalid tag "foo:bar": ` and the clauses read `tags must be of the form tag:<name> (e.g. tag:server)`, `the tag name (after 'tag:') is empty`, `tag names must start with a letter (after 'tag:')` and `tag names may contain only letters, digits, or '-'`. The merge message states that the message shape is aligned and that reading the port found no behavioural difference; the completion claim holds, the wording claim does not.

findings.title: --readonly does not select ReadOnlyServerMode for the served page
findings.detail: runWeb builds web.ServerOpts with Mode: web.LoginServerMode and overrides it with `if webArgs.readonly { opts.Mode = web.ReadOnlyServerMode }`, so the flag upstream decides two things: whether the tailscaled web client is started, and which of the two pages is served. The merged run_web threads --readonly only into the first of those; run_web_cgi and run_status_web take no mode and always serve the read-only page. `tnet web` without --readonly therefore turns the daemon pref on and then serves the same page `tnet web --readonly` serves, where `tailscale web` serves the login/management page. The merge message states the reason (this build's page is read-only either way), so this is a disclosed build gap rather than an oversight, but it is a divergence in the function the diff ports.

findings.title: --assert failure text is fork wording, not Go's
findings.detail: runIP's assertion failure is `fmt.Errorf("assertion failed: IP %q not found among %v", ipArgs.assert, ips)`, which quotes the value as typed and then lists the addresses the node actually holds — the list is the part that makes the failure diagnosable. The merged run_ip prints `assertion failed: this node does not hold <ip>`, naming neither the typed string nor the addresses. It also parses --assert first and refuses an unparseable value with `--assert: "x" is not a valid IP address`, where Go compares `ip.String() == ipArgs.assert` as strings and simply reports the assertion as failed. The diff's own message lists this as a known remainder.

findings.title: The mutually-exclusive-flags refusal keeps the `Error: ` prefix this diff removed elsewhere
findings.detail: cmd/tailscale/tailscale.go's main prints a returned error with `fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)` and exits 1, so `tailscale ip -1 -4` prints the bare sentence. The whole point of routing the empty-list and family errors through an explicit eprintln plus exit(1) in this diff was to drop the `Error: ` anyhow adds on the way out of main — but ip_usage_refusal is still raised with anyhow::bail!, so the one refusal that runs before any daemon round trip reads `Error: tnet ip -1, -4, and -6 are mutually exclusive`. A script matching on the text gets two different prefixes from the same command depending on which refusal it hit. The diff's own message lists this as a known remainder.
